Let $(M,g,N,o)$ be the smooth, boundaryless, oriented and time-oriented
Lorentzian four-manifold of [[def-emg-lorentzian-forms]], with signature
$(-,+,+,+)$, metric-selected connection $\nabla$ and oriented metric volume
form $\mathrm{vol}_g$. Let $F\in\Omega^2(M)$ be a smooth real two-form and
$j\in\Gamma(TM)$ a smooth vector field. Fix constants $\mu_0>0$ and $c>0$;
$\mu_0$ is a real coefficient here, and $c$ is the positive coordinate
conversion in $x^0=ct$ of [[def-emg-lorentzian-forms]]. Assume the mathematical
field equations

$$dF=0,\qquad \nabla_aF^{ab}=-\mu_0j^b.$$

The equations are conditional hypotheses, not physical postulates in this
mathematical item. Define $v\in\Gamma(TM)$ by $v^b:=\nabla_aF^{ab}$ and
define the current three-form by $\iota_j\mathrm{vol}_g$, the contraction
specified in [[def-gr-metric-volume-form-and-current-flux]]. Then:

**(a) Sign identity.** On $M$,

$$d(\star_gF)=-\iota_v\mathrm{vol}_g.$$

Consequently the sourced equation is equivalently

$$\nabla_aF^{ab}=-\mu_0j^b\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad d(\star_gF)=\mu_0\iota_j\mathrm{vol}_g.$$

**(b) Current conservation.** Either equivalent sourced equation implies
$\nabla_aj^a=0$. This conclusion requires the sourced equation and $\mu_0>0$;
it does not require $dF=0$.

**(c) Local component check.** At any $p\in M$, choose a positively oriented
point-normal chart supplied by
[[thm-gr-point-normal-and-exponential-coordinate-charts]]. In that chart,
write $E_i(x):=-cF_{0i}(x)$ and
$B_i(x):=\frac12\epsilon_{ijk}F_{jk}(x)$, where $\epsilon_{123}=+1$ and
$\epsilon_{ijk}$ is alternating. These are local component abbreviations in
the chosen chart, not global observer fields. With
$\operatorname{div}E:=\partial_iE_i$,
$(\operatorname{curl}E)_k:=\epsilon_{kij}\partial_iE_j$, and similarly
for $B$, the pointwise component identities are

$$v^0=-\frac{1}{c}\operatorname{div}E,\qquad v^k=\frac{1}{c^2}\partial_tE_k-(\operatorname{curl}B)_k,$$

$$ (d\star_gF)_{123}=\frac{1}{c}\operatorname{div}E,\qquad (d\star_gF)_{0ij}=\epsilon_{ijk}\left(\frac{1}{c^2}\partial_tE_k-(\operatorname{curl}B)_k\right),$$

$$ (dF)_{123}=\operatorname{div}B,\qquad (dF)_{0ij}=\frac{\epsilon_{ijk}}{c}\left(\partial_tB_k+(\operatorname{curl}E)_k\right),$$

where $\partial_t:=c\,\partial_0$. The equations are pointwise identities
in normal coordinates; they do not assert that these component abbreviations
form global three-vector fields on curved spacetime.

On an open flat Minkowski domain with a fixed inertial Cartesian chart
$x^0=ct$, define $\rho:=j^0/c$, $J^i:=j^i$, and
$\epsilon_0:=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$. The same component formulas at every point give

$$\operatorname{div}E=\frac{\rho}{\epsilon_0},\qquad \operatorname{curl}B-\frac{1}{c^2}\partial_tE=\mu_0J,\qquad \operatorname{div}B=0,\qquad \partial_tB+\operatorname{curl}E=0.$$

These are a coordinate reduction of the stated tensor and form equations, not
claims that the smooth fields describe an experiment.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]), let $M$ carry an orientation in the
sense of [[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]] (so that its
charts that are oriented in that orientation have orientation-preserving
transition maps), and let $\nabla$ be its metric-selected connection. This item
fixes the metric volume form, the flux of a current through oriented $3$-faces
and finite-chain charges. The orientation of $M$ is an independent datum: it is
not determined by the metric and not by the time orientation.

**(a) Metric volume density and volume form.** Let $(U,x)$ be an oriented
chart, with metric components $g_{ab}=g(\partial_a,\partial_b)$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]] clause (a)). Define the **metric volume
density**

$$w:=\sqrt{|\det(g_{ab})|}>0\qquad\text{on }U,$$

a strictly positive smooth function because $g_{ab}$ is smooth and
$g_p$ is nondegenerate. In the chart define the local $4$-form

$$\mathrm{vol}_{g,U}:=w\,dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3,$$

with the exterior product of [[def-wedge-product-of-differential-forms]] and the
coordinate covector fields of
[[prop-local-coordinate-expression-for-a-differential-form]]. That these local
forms agree on chart overlaps and therefore define one smooth nowhere-vanishing
$4$-form $\mathrm{vol}_g$ on $M$ — the **metric volume form** — is proved in
[[lem-gr-metric-volume-form-patching-and-face-normal]] clause (a), together
with the reading statement of clause (b) there: in every oriented chart
$\mathrm{vol}_g=w\,dx^0\wedge\cdots\wedge dx^3$, and on every positively
oriented $g_p$-orthonormal basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $T_pM$ one has
$\mathrm{vol}_{g,p}(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)=1$.

**(b) Current flux through oriented $3$-faces and chains.** Let $J$ be a
smooth vector field on $M$
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]). The **current
$3$-form** of $J$ is the contraction

$$\iota_J\mathrm{vol}_g,$$

the interior product of the $4$-form $\mathrm{vol}_g$ with $J$
([[def-interior-product-of-a-form-by-a-vector-field]]).

By a **smooth singular $k$-simplex** of $M$ — the convention of the library
definition `def-smooth-singular-simplex` (differential-geometry track),
restated here so this page is self-contained — we mean a map
$\sigma:\Delta^k\to M$ whose domain is the standard $k$-simplex
$$\Delta^k=\Bigl\{t\in\mathbb R^{k+1}:t_i\ge0,\ \textstyle\sum_it_i=1\Bigr\},$$
for which there exist an open set $O\subseteq A^k=\{t\in\mathbb R^{k+1}:\sum_it_i=1\}$
containing $\Delta^k$ and a smooth map $\bar\sigma:O\to M$ with
$\bar\sigma|_{\Delta^k}=\sigma$; the extension is not part of the simplex
data, and degenerate parametrizations are allowed. With the integration of
forms over such simplices
([[def-integral-of-a-form-over-a-smooth-singular-simplex]]), a **$3$-face** is
a smooth singular $3$-simplex $\sigma$, and the **flux of $J$ through
$\sigma$** is the real number

$$\Phi_J(\sigma):=\int_\sigma\iota_J\mathrm{vol}_g.$$

A **finite smooth singular $k$-chain** — the convention of the library
definition `def-smooth-singular-chain-and-cochain-complexes`, restated here —
is a finite formal real linear combination $\Sigma=\sum_i c_i\sigma_i$ of
smooth singular $k$-simplices. For such a $3$-chain the **flux of $J$ through
$\Sigma$** is defined additively,

$$\Phi_J(\Sigma):=\sum_i c_i\,\Phi_J(\sigma_i),$$

a definition independent of the written expression for $\Sigma$, because a
finite formal sum is evaluated by adding the finitely many coefficients and
inserting a zero coefficient changes nothing. $\Phi_J(\Sigma)$ is the **charge**
of the current $J$ assigned to $\Sigma$ when the model reads $J$ as a conserved
current; that reading belongs to the physical postulates and is not part of
this definition.

**(c) Non-null faces and their unit normals.** A $3$-dimensional linear subspace
$H\subseteq T_pM$ is **nondegenerate** for $g_p$ when the restriction of $g_p$
to $H$ is nondegenerate, equivalently when $H\cap H^\perp=\{0\}$ in the
orthogonality of [[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]. A
smooth singular $3$-simplex $\sigma$ is **non-null at** a parameter point $t$
when the span of the three velocity vectors
$\sigma_*\partial_1|_t,\sigma_*\partial_2|_t,\sigma_*\partial_3|_t$ has
dimension $3$ and is nondegenerate at $\sigma(t)$, and **non-null** when this holds at every
parameter point. For a non-null face the **unit normal** $\nu$ at that point is
the unique vector of $T_{\sigma(t)}M$ with $\nu\in H^\perp$,
$g(\nu,\nu)\in\{-1,+1\}$ and $(\nu,\sigma_*\partial_1,\sigma_*\partial_2,
\sigma_*\partial_3)$ a positively oriented basis of $T_{\sigma(t)}M$; its
existence, uniqueness and its sign $\varepsilon:=g(\nu,\nu)$ are proved in
[[lem-gr-metric-volume-form-patching-and-face-normal]] clause (c), together
with the density identity of clause (c) used to read $\iota_J\mathrm{vol}_g$ on
such a face. Rank-deficient faces and rank-three faces with degenerate induced
metric are not assigned a unit normal; their flux is defined
by the $3$-form $\iota_J\mathrm{vol}_g$ itself, as in clause (b).

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold, possibly with boundary. For $k\ge1$, $c\in C_k^\infty(M;\mathbb R)$ and $\omega\in\Omega^{k-1}(M)$, define integration over a chain by the finite linear sum of its simplex integrals. Then
$$\int_c d\omega=\int_{\partial c}\omega.$$
The zero chain has integral zero. In degree zero the boundary is zero; no degree-minus-one form is required by this statement.

Let $L_1,L_2,L_3>0$ be real periods, let
$\Lambda:=L_1\mathbb Z\times L_2\mathbb Z\times L_3\mathbb Z\subseteq\mathbb R^3$,
and let $q:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb T^3_L:=\mathbb R^3/\Lambda$ be the quotient
map with the quotient topology. Then $q$ is a smooth local diffeomorphism and
$\mathbb T^3_L$ is a compact,
Hausdorff, second-countable smooth three-manifold without boundary.

The forms $dx^1,dx^2,dx^3$ and coordinate vector fields
$\partial_1,\partial_2,\partial_3$ on $\mathbb R^3$ descend to global smooth
forms and vector fields on $\mathbb T^3_L$. Every smooth $\Lambda$-periodic
function on $\mathbb R^3$ descends to a smooth function on $\mathbb T^3_L$.
Consequently, $M_L:=\mathbb R_{x^0}\times\mathbb T^3_L$ has a smooth,
boundaryless four-manifold structure and carries the smooth Lorentzian metric,
orientation, and time orientation

$$g:=-(dx^0)^2+(dx^1)^2+(dx^2)^2+(dx^3)^2,\qquad N:=\partial_0,\qquad o:=dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3.$$

In the product charts from the quotient atlas the metric has constant matrix
$\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ and its metric-selected Christoffel symbols
vanish.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a time-oriented smooth Lorentzian four-manifold
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]), let $M$ carry an orientation in the
sense of [[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]] (so that its
charts that are oriented in that orientation have orientation-preserving
transition maps), and let $\nabla$ be its metric-selected connection. This item
fixes the metric volume form, the flux of a current through oriented $3$-faces
and finite-chain charges. The orientation of $M$ is an independent datum: it is
not determined by the metric and not by the time orientation.

**(a) Metric volume density and volume form.** Let $(U,x)$ be an oriented
chart, with metric components $g_{ab}=g(\partial_a,\partial_b)$
([[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]] clause (a)). Define the **metric volume
density**

$$w:=\sqrt{|\det(g_{ab})|}>0\qquad\text{on }U,$$

a strictly positive smooth function because $g_{ab}$ is smooth and
$g_p$ is nondegenerate. In the chart define the local $4$-form

$$\mathrm{vol}_{g,U}:=w\,dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3,$$

with the exterior product of [[def-wedge-product-of-differential-forms]] and the
coordinate covector fields of
[[prop-local-coordinate-expression-for-a-differential-form]]. That these local
forms agree on chart overlaps and therefore define one smooth nowhere-vanishing
$4$-form $\mathrm{vol}_g$ on $M$ — the **metric volume form** — is proved in
[[lem-gr-metric-volume-form-patching-and-face-normal]] clause (a), together
with the reading statement of clause (b) there: in every oriented chart
$\mathrm{vol}_g=w\,dx^0\wedge\cdots\wedge dx^3$, and on every positively
oriented $g_p$-orthonormal basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ of $T_pM$ one has
$\mathrm{vol}_{g,p}(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)=1$.

smooth vector field on $M$
([[def-smooth-vector-field-as-a-tangent-bundle-section]]). The **current
$3$-form** of $J$ is the contraction

$$\iota_J\mathrm{vol}_g,$$

the interior product of the $4$-form $\mathrm{vol}_g$ with $J$
([[def-interior-product-of-a-form-by-a-vector-field]]).

By a **smooth singular $k$-simplex** of $M$ — the convention of the library
definition `def-smooth-singular-simplex` (differential-geometry track),
restated here so this page is self-contained — we mean a map
$\sigma:\Delta^k\to M$ whose domain is the standard $k$-simplex
$$\Delta^k=\Bigl\{t\in\mathbb R^{k+1}:t_i\ge0,\ \textstyle\sum_it_i=1\Bigr\},$$
for which there exist an open set $O\subseteq A^k=\{t\in\mathbb R^{k+1}:\sum_it_i=1\}$
containing $\Delta^k$ and a smooth map $\bar\sigma:O\to M$ with
$\bar\sigma|_{\Delta^k}=\sigma$; the extension is not part of the simplex
data, and degenerate parametrizations are allowed. With the integration of
forms over such simplices
([[def-integral-of-a-form-over-a-smooth-singular-simplex]]), a **$3$-face** is
a smooth singular $3$-simplex $\sigma$, and the **flux of $J$ through
$\sigma$** is the real number

$$\Phi_J(\sigma):=\int_\sigma\iota_J\mathrm{vol}_g.$$

A **finite smooth singular $k$-chain** — the convention of the library
definition `def-smooth-singular-chain-and-cochain-complexes`, restated here —
is a finite formal real linear combination $\Sigma=\sum_i c_i\sigma_i$ of
smooth singular $k$-simplices. For such a $3$-chain the **flux of $J$ through
$\Sigma$** is defined additively,

$$\Phi_J(\Sigma):=\sum_i c_i\,\Phi_J(\sigma_i),$$

a definition independent of the written expression for $\Sigma$, because a
finite formal sum is evaluated by adding the finitely many coefficients and
inserting a zero coefficient changes nothing. $\Phi_J(\Sigma)$ is the **charge**
of the current $J$ assigned to $\Sigma$ when the model reads $J$ as a conserved
current; that reading belongs to the physical postulates and is not part of
this definition.

**(c) Non-null faces and their unit normals.** A $3$-dimensional linear subspace
$H\subseteq T_pM$ is **nondegenerate** for $g_p$ when the restriction of $g_p$
to $H$ is nondegenerate, equivalently when $H\cap H^\perp=\{0\}$ in the
orthogonality of [[def-lorentz-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]. A
smooth singular $3$-simplex $\sigma$ is **non-null at** a parameter point $t$
when the span of the three velocity vectors
$\sigma_*\partial_1|_t,\sigma_*\partial_2|_t,\sigma_*\partial_3|_t$ has
dimension $3$ and is nondegenerate at $\sigma(t)$, and **non-null** when this holds at every
parameter point. For a non-null face the **unit normal** $\nu$ at that point is
the unique vector of $T_{\sigma(t)}M$ with $\nu\in H^\perp$,
$g(\nu,\nu)\in\{-1,+1\}$ and $(\nu,\sigma_*\partial_1,\sigma_*\partial_2,
\sigma_*\partial_3)$ a positively oriented basis of $T_{\sigma(t)}M$; its
existence, uniqueness and its sign $\varepsilon:=g(\nu,\nu)$ are proved in
[[lem-gr-metric-volume-form-patching-and-face-normal]] clause (c), together
with the density identity of clause (c) used to read $\iota_J\mathrm{vol}_g$ on
such a face. Rank-deficient faces and rank-three faces with degenerate induced
metric are not assigned a unit normal; their flux is defined
by the $3$-form $\iota_J\mathrm{vol}_g$ itself, as in clause (b).

four-manifold of [[def-emg-lorentzian-forms]], let
$F\in\Omega^2(M)$ and $j\in\Gamma(TM)$ be smooth, and fix constants
$c,\mu_0>0$. Assume
$dF=0$ and $\nabla_aF^{ab}=-\mu_0j^b$, equivalently
$d(\star_gF)=\mu_0\iota_j\mathrm{vol}_g$ by
[[lem-emg-maxwell-current-forms]]. A finite smooth singular $k$-chain means
a finite formal real linear combination of smooth singular $k$-simplices,
with the boundary operation of
[[def-gr-metric-volume-form-and-current-flux]] and
[[thm-stokes-theorem-for-smooth-singular-chains]].

For a finite smooth singular three-chain $\Sigma$, define its charge by

$$Q(\Sigma):=\frac1c\int_\Sigma\iota_j\mathrm{vol}_g.$$

Then:

**(a) Gauss charge formula.** For every such $\Sigma$,

$$Q(\Sigma)=\frac{1}{\mu_0c}\int_{\partial\Sigma}\star_gF.$$

Consequently, if $\partial\Sigma=0$, then $Q(\Sigma)=0$. This is the
compact-cycle neutrality constraint for a smooth everywhere-defined sourced
field.

**(b) Bounding-surface restriction.** For every finite smooth singular
three-chain $V$, the magnetic flux through its boundary vanishes:

$$\int_{\partial V}F=0.$$

The equation $dF=0$ does not imply that the flux through every closed
two-cycle is zero; this item gives a zero-flux conclusion only when the cycle
is the boundary of a finite smooth chain in the field domain. Likewise, the
electric flux formula in (a) identifies charge with flux only for a bounding
surface.

$\partial C=\Sigma_2-\Sigma_1+B$ for three-chains
$\Sigma_1,\Sigma_2,B$, then

$$Q(\Sigma_2)-Q(\Sigma_1)=-Q(B).$$

Equal charge on the two slices therefore requires zero net side flux. No
asymptotic charge or flux at infinity is asserted; noncompact limits require
separate convergence and boundary-flux hypotheses.

Let $(M,g,N)$ be a smooth, Hausdorff, second-countable four-manifold without boundary, with smooth Lorentzian metric $g$ of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ and smooth time-orientation field $N$, as in [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]. Supply an independent orientation $o$ of $M$ in the sense of [[def-oriented-smooth-manifold-and-oriented-chart]]. The metric and time orientation do not select $o$. Write $\mathrm{vol}_g$ for the oriented metric volume form of [[def-gr-metric-volume-form-and-current-flux]]; in any positively oriented chart it has components $\sqrt{|\det(g_{ab})|}\,dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3$.

A smooth real $k$-form is a smooth section of $\bigwedge^kT^*M$, and its space is denoted $\Omega^k(M)$, as in [[def-smooth-differential-k-form]]. In this page, $F\in\Omega^2(M)$ means an arbitrary smooth real two-form. No equation such as $dF=0$, no global potential, and no physical field law is included in this definition.

An **observer at $p\in M$** is a vector $n\in T_pM$ with $g_p(n,n)=-1$ and $g_p(n,N_p)<0$; its **rest space** is $n^\perp=\{v:g_p(v,n)=0\}$, as in [[def-gr-observer-and-rest-space]]. A smooth **observer congruence** on an open set $U\subseteq M$ is a smooth vector field whose value at every point is an observer. Its observer curves are the maximal integral curves, and a chart is adapted to it when its three spatial coordinate functions are constant along those curves, as in [[def-gr-observer-congruence-and-adapted-charts]]. Such a congruence need not be hypersurface-orthogonal.

A **local frame field** on $U$ is an ordered smooth basis field of $TM|_U$. A **coordinate frame** is the basis of coordinate vector fields supplied by a chart. A **tetrad field** is a local frame $(E_0,E_1,E_2,E_3)$ with $g(E_A,E_B)=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)_{AB}$; it is future-directed when $E_0$ is future-directed, as in [[def-gr-local-frame-and-tetrad-fields]]. These are distinct objects: an observer congruence is a vector field, an adapted chart is a coordinate chart, and a tetrad is a basis field. A tetrad field is not presumed to be a coordinate frame. For every observer congruence $n$, each point has a neighborhood carrying an $n$-adapted tetrad; this is a local assertion only.

A **worldline** on this Lorentzian manifold means a $C^1$ or piecewise-$C^1$ regular curve with future-timelike tangent and specified interval domain, as defined precisely in [[def-gr-timelike-worldline-and-proper-time]]. Its parameter is arbitrary; the proper-time and four-velocity constructions of that definition apply under their stated hypotheses. A worldline is a mathematical curve here and does not assert the existence or motion of a physical body.

For coordinate bookkeeping only, when a chart is chosen with all four coordinate values assigned the metre, write $x^0=ct$, where $t$ is assigned seconds and $c>0$ is the corresponding scale in $\mathrm m\,\mathrm s^{-1}$. Then $g_{ab}$ is recorded as dimensionless. This is a unit convention on a chart, not a claim that the chart is inertial, orthonormal, global, or physically realized; $c$ in this mathematical convention has no asserted measured value.

Use the unique torsion-free metric-compatible connection $\nabla^g$ and the curvature convention of [[def-gr-metric-selected-connection]] and [[thm-gr-curvature-tensoriality-and-coordinate-formula]]. In a length-coordinate chart, the displayed Christoffel formula differentiates dimensionless metric components once, so $\Gamma^a{}_{bc}$ is recorded in $\mathrm m^{-1}$. The curvature coordinate formula contains one derivative of $\Gamma$ or a product of two $\Gamma$ components, so $R^a{}_{bcd}$ and its Ricci and scalar contractions are recorded in $\mathrm m^{-2}$. These component assignments apply only in length-coordinate charts; other coordinate units transform by their Jacobians.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

For a smooth manifold $M$, possibly with boundary, let
$$C_k^\infty(M;\mathbb R)=\mathbb R^{(S_k^\infty(M))}\quad(k\ge0),\qquad C_k^\infty(M;\mathbb R)=0\quad(k<0),$$
using [[def-smooth-singular-simplex]]. It is the subspace of [[def-real-singular-chain-complex]] spanned by the smooth simplices, with the same signed face differential.

This is a subcomplex: an affine face map $\delta_i:A^{k-1}\to A^k$ has the open inverse image $\delta_i^{-1}(O)$ containing $\Delta^{k-1}$. Composing $\bar\sigma$ with this affine map on that inverse image extends $\sigma\delta_i$ smoothly into $M$. Thus every face is smooth, and the already proved signed cancellation gives $\partial^2=0$ on this subspace.

Define the **smooth singular cochain complex** by
$$C_\infty^k(M;\mathbb R)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb R}(C_k^\infty(M;\mathbb R),\mathbb R),\qquad \delta\varphi=\varphi\partial.$$
As for [[def-real-singular-cochain-complex]], these are arbitrary real functions on the supplied smooth-simplex basis, evaluated by finite sums. Precomposition gives $\delta^2\varphi=\varphi\partial^2=0$. Define $H_k^\infty(M;\mathbb R)=\ker\partial_k/\operatorname{im}\partial_{k+1}$ and $H_\infty^k(M;\mathbb R)=\ker\delta^k/\operatorname{im}\delta^{k-1}$; both quotients are licensed by square-zero.

Negative groups vanish and the degree-zero boundary is zero. On a point all simplices are smooth, so the complexes are the ordinary unnormalized point complexes; no constant simplices are discarded. For the empty manifold all groups are zero. The specified subspaces and duals require no choice of extensions or bases.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\sin x:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^nx^{2n+1}}{(2n+1)!},\qquad\cos x:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^nx^{2n}}{(2n)!}.$$

These are real power series in the sense of [[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]. Their convergence for every real argument is discharged by [[lem-sine-and-cosine-series-converge-everywhere]].

For every real $x$, both series
$$\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^n x^{2n+1}}{(2n+1)!}\quad\text{and}\quad\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^n x^{2n}}{(2n)!}$$
converge absolutely. Equivalently, both power series have infinite radius of convergence.

Let

$$f(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}a_n(x-c)^n$$

have radius $R$. For every $x$ with $|x-c|<R$, the function $f$ is differentiable at $x$ ([[def-derivative]]) and

$$f'(x)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\iota(n+1)a_{n+1}(x-c)^n.$$

The differentiated series has the same radius $R$.

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

For every real $x$,
$$\sin x=0\Longleftrightarrow x=m\pi\text{ for some }m\in\mathbb Z,\qquad \cos x=0\Longleftrightarrow x=(m+1/2)\pi\text{ for some }m\in\mathbb Z.$$
Both sine and cosine have period $2\pi$, and no smaller positive number is a common period.

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be bounded
([[def-bounded-set]]). Write $\mathcal{P}$ for the set of all partitions of
$[a,b]$ ([[def-partition-and-refinement]]) and put

$$\mathcal{L} \;:=\; \{\, L(f,P) \ : \ P \in \mathcal{P} \,\}, \qquad \mathcal{U} \;:=\; \{\, U(f,P) \ : \ P \in \mathcal{P} \,\}$$

for the sets of lower and of upper Darboux sums ([[def-darboux-sums]]).

### Both extrema exist

**$\mathcal{P}$ is nonempty**: the pair $(1, t)$ with $t_0 := a$ and $t_k := b$
for $k \ge 1$ is a partition of $[a,b]$, since $a < b$. So $\mathcal{L}$ and
$\mathcal{U}$ are nonempty.

**$\mathcal{L}$ is bounded above and $\mathcal{U}$ is bounded below.** Fix any
$Q \in \mathcal{P}$. By claim 2 of [[lem-refinement-inequalities]],
$L(f,P) \le U(f,Q)$ for every $P \in \mathcal{P}$, so $U(f,Q)$ is an upper bound
of $\mathcal{L}$; and $L(f,Q) \le U(f,P)$ for every $P$, so $L(f,Q)$ is a lower
bound of $\mathcal{U}$.

Hence a nonempty set bounded above has a supremum
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) and a nonempty set bounded below has an infimum
([[thm-infimum-property]], [[def-infimum]]), each unique ([[lem-sup-unique]]).
The **lower** and **upper Darboux integrals** of $f$ over $[a,b]$ are the real
numbers

$$\underline{\int_a^b} f \;:=\; \sup \mathcal{L} \;=\; \sup_{P} L(f,P), \qquad \overline{\int_a^b} f \;:=\; \inf \mathcal{U} \;=\; \inf_{P} U(f,P) .$$

### The lower integral never exceeds the upper one

$$\underline{\int_a^b} f \;\le\; \overline{\int_a^b} f .$$

Indeed, for each fixed $Q \in \mathcal{P}$ the number $U(f,Q)$ is an upper bound
of $\mathcal{L}$, so the least upper bound satisfies
$\underline{\int_a^b} f \le U(f,Q)$. As $Q$ was arbitrary, $\underline{\int_a^b}f$
is a lower bound of $\mathcal{U}$, and the greatest lower bound satisfies
$\underline{\int_a^b} f \le \overline{\int_a^b} f$ ([[def-infimum]]).

Moreover, for **every** partition $P$,

$$L(f,P) \;\le\; \underline{\int_a^b} f \;\le\; \overline{\int_a^b} f \;\le\; U(f,P) ,$$

the outer inequalities because a member of a set is at most its supremum and at
least its infimum.

### Integrability

$f$ is **Darboux integrable on $[a,b]$**, and on this page simply
**integrable**, when

$$\underline{\int_a^b} f \;=\; \overline{\int_a^b} f ,$$

and then the common value is written

$$\int_a^b f \qquad \text{or} \qquad \int_a^b f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x ,$$

the **integral of $f$ over $[a,b]$**. It is a single well-determined real
number, being the common value of two numbers each of which is unique
([[lem-sup-unique]]). Without the displayed equality the symbol $\int_a^b f$ is
not defined and is never written.

**The inequality above is the whole difficulty.** By the previous paragraph
integrability is *never* a question of one integral exceeding the other, only of
the gap $\overline{\int_a^b} f - \underline{\int_a^b} f \ge 0$ being $0$; and by
[[thm-riemann-criterion]] that gap is $0$ exactly when a single partition can be
found making $U(f,P) - L(f,P)$ small. Whether that is possible is settled
completely, in terms of the discontinuities of $f$, by
[[thm-lebesgue-criterion]].

**"Riemann integrable" means the same thing here.** The definition above is
Darboux's. Riemann's own definition, in terms of tagged partitions of small
mesh, is [[def-tagged-partition-and-riemann-sum]], and the two define the same
class of functions with the same integral by [[thm-darboux-equals-riemann]].
Until that theorem is proved the two phrases are kept apart; after it they are
used interchangeably, as they are throughout the literature.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

Let $\sigma:\Delta^k\to M$ be a smooth singular simplex and let $\omega$ be a smooth $k$-form on an open neighbourhood of its image in $M$. For $k\ge1$ put
$$T_k=\{x\in\mathbb R^k:x_j\ge0,\ \sum_jx_j\le1\},\qquad a(x)=v_0+\sum_{j=1}^kx_j(v_j-v_0).$$
Take a smooth extension $\bar\sigma$ near $\Delta^k$, restrict its domain so that $\omega$ is defined on its image, and write $a^*\bar\sigma^*\omega=f(x)\,dx_1\wedge\cdots\wedge dx_k$. Define
$$\int_\sigma\omega:=\int_{T_k}f(x)\,dx.$$
The right side is the Jordan-set Riemann integral. In degree zero define $\int_\sigma\omega=\omega(\sigma(v_0))$. This fixes the positive point convention. Reversing the domain orientation negates the integral. Independence of other positive affine coordinates is the forward justification [[lem-simplex-integrals-are-independent-of-affine-coordinate-identification]].

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $g:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be injective and $C^1$, and suppose $Dg(x)$ is invertible for every $x\in U$. Let $K\subseteq U$ be compact and Jordan measurable. For a bounded function $f:g(K)\to\mathbb R$, the following are equivalent:

1. $f$ is Riemann integrable on $g(K)$;
2. $x\mapsto f(g(x))|\det Dg(x)|$ is Riemann integrable on $K$.

When either condition holds,
$$\int_{g(K)}f(y)\,dy=\int_K f(g(x))|\det Dg(x)|\,dx.$$

A metric-bounded set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is Jordan measurable if and only
if its boundary $\partial E$ is null, equivalently has content zero.
Let $m\ge1$, let $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be a closed nondegenerate rectangle, and let $f:Q\to\mathbb R$ be continuous. Its graph has content zero in $\mathbb R^{m+1}$.
Every continuous real function on a compact Jordan measurable set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is Riemann integrable over $E$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Fix $m\ge1$. A **closed cube** is a rectangle $\prod_{j<m}[a_j,a_j+\ell]$ with $\ell\ge0$; its volume is $\ell^m$. A set $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is **null** when, for every $\varepsilon>0$, it is covered by a sequence of closed cubes whose nonnegative volume series converges with sum at most $\varepsilon$. It has **content zero** when such a cover can be finite.

The series and finite sums are [[def-series]] and [[def-finite-sum]], and their nonnegative bounds use [[thm-nonnegative-series-bounded-partial-sums]] and [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. Both properties pass to subsets. Padding a finite cover with degenerate zero-volume cubes proves that content zero implies null. This terminology defines only cover-nullity; it does not define a measure on arbitrary sets.

Let $m\ge1$, let $A\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be bounded and Jordan measurable, let $N\ge1$, and let $A_1,\ldots,A_N\subseteq A$ be bounded Jordan measurable sets such that $A_i\cap A_j$ has content zero whenever $i\ne j$ and such that $A\setminus\bigcup_{i=1}^NA_i$ has content zero. Let $f:A\to\mathbb R$ be bounded, Riemann integrable over $A$ and Riemann integrable over each $A_i$. Then

$$\int_Af=\sum_{i=1}^N\int_{A_i}f.$$
Every continuous real function on a closed nondegenerate rectangle $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $m\ge1$, is Riemann integrable.

Let $A\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $B\subseteq\mathbb R^q$ be nondegenerate closed rectangles, and let $f:A\times B\to\mathbb R$ be Riemann integrable. Then the four lower and upper section-integral functions of [[def-sections-and-iterated-riemann-integrals]] are Riemann integrable and
$$\int_A\ell_B=\int_Au_B=\int_{A\times B}f=\int_B\ell_A=\int_Bu_A.$$

If the $B$-sections are integrable outside a content-zero set $N\subseteq A$, every bounded exceptionally completed function $h$ with $h(x)=\int_Bf_x$ for $x\notin N$ is integrable and
$$\int_{A\times B}f=\int_Ah.$$
The same assertion holds with the coordinate blocks exchanged. In particular, when every section in an order is integrable, the ordinary iterated integral in that order exists and equals the multiple integral. The theorem does not assert that every section of an integrable function is integrable.

For a bounded function $f:Q\to\mathbb R$ on a nondegenerate rectangle
$Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, define
$$\underline{\int_Q}f:=\sup_P L(f,P),\qquad \overline{\int_Q}f:=\inf_P U(f,P),$$
over all grid partitions $P$ of $Q$. The grid family is nonempty, since the endpoints in each coordinate give a one-cell grid. Every lower sum is at most every upper sum by a common refinement and [[lem-multidimensional-refinement-inequalities]], so the two sets of sums are nonempty and bounded and the extrema exist ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[thm-infimum-property]], [[def-infimum]], [[lem-sup-unique]]).

The function is **Riemann integrable over $Q$** when the two values agree.
Their unique common real is $\int_Q f$. No integral is defined here for a
degenerate rectangle, because the grid definition requires every coordinate
interval to have distinct endpoints. This is the multidimensional Darboux
definition; its agreement with the published one-dimensional definition is
proved separately.

Fix a natural number $m\ge1$. For $a,b\in\mathbb R^m$ with $a_j\le b_j$ for $j<m$, define
$$[a,b]:=\{x\in\mathbb R^m:a_j\le x_j\le b_j\ (j<m)\},\qquad \operatorname{vol}[a,b]:=\prod_{j<m}(b_j-a_j).$$
The product is the recursively defined finite product of [[def-finite-sum]]. The rectangle is **nondegenerate** when every $a_j<b_j$, and it is a **cube** when all side lengths are equal.

Every factor is nonnegative, so volume is nonnegative. For a coordinate index $r<m$, cutting at $c\in[a_r,b_r]$ gives two rectangles whose volumes add to the original, by distributivity in that factor and [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. Under the standard identification $\mathbb R^1\cong\mathbb R$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]), this is the interval $[a_0,b_0]$ and its length.

derivations.claim:
For a fixed permutation $\sigma$, the barycentric coordinates of a point
in the ordered region
$0\le u_{\sigma(3)}\le u_{\sigma(2)}\le u_{\sigma(1)}\le1$ relative to its
four listed vertices are $1-u_{\sigma(1)}$,
$u_{\sigma(1)}-u_{\sigma(2)}$, $u_{\sigma(2)}-u_{\sigma(3)}$, and
$u_{\sigma(3)}$; these are nonnegative, sum to one, and reconstruct the
point. Thus the six tetrahedra cover the cube with disjoint interiors. Each
affine map is smooth on a neighbourhood of its standard simplex, and its
composition with the smooth quotient map [F1] is a smooth singular simplex.
The ordered edge determinant is
$L_1L_2L_3\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)$, so the weight
$\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)$ orients each tetrahedron by
$dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3$.

The function $h$ is periodic and smooth, with $h'=f$ by [F6]–[F7], so
$F$ and $j$ are smooth global fields on the product. Since
$dF=-\mu_0h'(x^1)dx^1\wedge dx^0\wedge dx^1=0$, the homogeneous equation
holds. Raising indices gives $F^{01}=\mu_0h$ and $F^{10}=-\mu_0h$. Thus
$\nabla_aF^{a0}=\partial_1F^{10}=-\mu_0f=-\mu_0j^0$,
$\nabla_aF^{a1}=\partial_0F^{01}=0=-\mu_0j^1$, and the $b=2,3$ equations
have both sides zero. Thus both field equations are verified everywhere.

An internal facet arises by setting one adjacent-coordinate inequality
to equality. The two permutations differ by swapping those adjacent entries;
their omitted vertices occupy the same position in the ordered vertex lists,
and the remaining three vertices have the same order. Thus the face maps in
[F5] are identical, while the permutation signs are opposite. Their two
coefficients in the signed face boundary therefore sum to zero. This covers
both internal facet types (equal first and second coordinates, or equal
second and third coordinates).

Fix a coordinate $i$ and order the other two indices as $(a,b)$. The
triangle on $x^i=L_i$ comes from permutation $(i,a,b)$ by omitting vertex
$0$; its ordered vertices are $L_ie_i$, $L_ie_i+L_ae_a$, and
$L_ie_i+L_ae_a+L_be_b$. The triangle on $x^i=0$ comes from $(a,b,i)$ by
omitting the final vertex; its ordered vertices are $0$, $L_ae_a$, and
$L_ae_a+L_be_b$. Translation by $L_ie_i$ makes these vertex lists identical,
so their quotient face maps are equal. Moving $i$ from first to last is two
transpositions, so the permutation coefficients agree; the omitted-vertex
boundary signs are $+1$ and $-1$. By [F5] the corresponding face terms
cancel. This pairs every outer triangle, for all three coordinates and both
orders $(a,b)$.

The finite chain boundary is the alternating face sum in [F5]. Steps 2.1
and 2.2 cancel every internal and external face term, respectively. Hence
$\partial\Sigma=0$, as required in [F3]. The explicit finite triangulation
adds no choice, as [F4] records.

Since $\partial\Sigma=0$ by step 3.1, the finite-chain neutrality
result [F3] applies and gives $Q(\Sigma)=0$.

Let $C=[0,L_1]\times[0,L_2]\times[0,L_3]$ and let $T_\sigma\subset C$
be the affine tetrahedron with the ordered vertices specified in the Example;
each $T_\sigma$ is closed and bounded, hence compact by [F9], so the
continuous function $f$ is bounded there. The standard $T_3$ is compact
Jordan by [F8].
Write $\phi_\sigma:T_3\to T_\sigma$ for its affine parametrization and
$\psi_\sigma=q\circ\phi_\sigma$ for the corresponding simplex in $M$.
Since $j=f(x^1)\partial_0$ and $\mathrm{vol}_g=dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3$ by [F1], the interior-product definition in [F2] gives
$\iota_j\mathrm{vol}_g=f(x^1)dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3$. The pullback of
$\iota_j\mathrm{vol}_g$ by
$\psi_\sigma$ has coefficient
$f(\phi_\sigma^1(s))\det D\phi_\sigma$ in the standard positive affine
coordinates, because the descended coordinate forms pull back under $q$ to
the Euclidean coordinate forms [F1]. By [F8] this is the coefficient whose
integral defines $\int_{\psi_\sigma}\iota_j\mathrm{vol}_g$. This coefficient
is continuous on compact Jordan $T_3$, hence integrable by [F9]. The determinant
of the three edge vectors is
$\det D\phi_\sigma=L_1L_2L_3\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)$, so the chain
coefficient gives
$$\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\int_{\psi_\sigma}\iota_j\mathrm{vol}_g
=\int_{T_3} f(\phi_\sigma^1(s))|\det D\phi_\sigma|\,ds
=\int_{T_\sigma}f(x^1)\,dx^1dx^2dx^3.$$
The last equality is [F8]'s change-of-variables formula: $T_3$ is compact
Jordan, $\phi_\sigma$ extends to an injective affine $C^1$ map on
$\mathbb R^3$ with nonsingular constant derivative, and $f$ is bounded and
continuous on $T_\sigma$.

The cube $C$ and each $T_\sigma$ are closed and bounded, hence compact by
Heine--Borel, and they are bounded Jordan sets. Indeed their
boundaries are finite unions of bounded pieces of affine planes; each such
piece is contained in the graph of an affine function over a containing
closed nondegenerate rectangle after solving the plane equation for a
coordinate with nonzero normal component. These graphs have content zero by
[F9], so the boundary criterion in [F9] applies. By step 1.1 the six
$T_\sigma$ cover $C$ and have disjoint interiors. Thus each pairwise
intersection is contained in the union of their boundaries and has content
zero by finite-union and subset closure in [F9], while the remainder
$C\setminus\bigcup_{\sigma\in S_3}T_\sigma$ is
empty. The coefficient $f$ is continuous and bounded on the compact Jordan
sets $C,T_\sigma$, so all integrals in the finite additivity hypotheses are
defined by [F9]. Applying the finite Jordan-set additivity result in [F9]
and using the chain definition in [F2] gives
$$Q(\Sigma)=\frac1c\sum_{\sigma\in S_3}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)
\int_{\psi_\sigma}\iota_j\mathrm{vol}_g
=\frac1c\int_C f(x^1)\,dx^1dx^2dx^3.$$

Write $A=[0,L_1]$ and $B=[0,L_2]\times[0,L_3]$, so $C=A\times B$.
The coefficient $f(x^1)$ is continuous on $C$ and hence integrable there by
[F10]. Rectangular Fubini [F10] applies, and its sections over $B$ are the
constant function $f(x^1)$. The multidimensional Darboux sums and volume
formula in [F10] therefore give
$$\int_Cf(x^1)\,dx^1dx^2dx^3
=L_2L_3\int_0^{L_1}f(x^1)\,dx^1.$$
By [F7], $h'=f$ and the one-dimensional FTC gives
$\int_0^{L_1}f(x^1)\,dx^1=h(L_1)-h(0)=0$, since the sine values at $0$ and
$2\pi$ agree. Hence the direct integral computation also yields
$Q(\Sigma)=0$, in agreement with step 4.1.
